```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(deconflate)
```

The package assumes no species, outcome or unit. A model needs the same
three things anywhere: how common each disease is, how the diseases go
together, and the impact estimates of one outcome. This vignette shows two
settings outside dairy cattle: four respiratory diseases of growing pigs
with three outcomes, and four chronic conditions in people with an event
outcome.

**All values here are made up to illustrate the package.** They are
plausible in size but are not estimates from the literature, and the
results say nothing about these diseases.

## Pigs: PRRS and the respiratory disease complex

Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome (PRRS) rarely comes alone:
it weakens the lungs' defences, and pigs with PRRS are more often
infected with porcine circovirus type 2 (PCV2), *Mycoplasma
hyopneumoniae* (MHP, enzootic pneumonia) and swine influenza (SIV). A
study of one disease at a time therefore measures part of the others'
effect as well, and adding up such estimates counts that part more than
once.

The inputs are in the installed folder `pigs`, as CSV files: one diseases
table, one associations table and one impact table per outcome. Every value
refers to the same period (the grow-finish period) and population. What
each impact table is about and its units are given when it is read
(`outcome` and `units`, both optional); they are used in the printouts and
the plots.

```{r}
pigs <- system.file("extdata", "pigs", package = "deconflate")
list.files(pigs)
read_pigs <- function(impacts, outcome = NULL, units = NULL) {
  cm_read_inputs(diseases = file.path(pigs, "diseases.csv"),
                 associations = file.path(pigs, "associations.csv"),
                 impacts = file.path(pigs, impacts), outcome = outcome, units = units)
}
```

The associations table has five of the six pairs; no row mentions PCV2 and
SIV, so the model fills in that association from the others (and lists it
in `$unknown_pairs`):

```{r}
adg <- read_pigs("impacts_adg.csv", outcome = "average daily gain loss", units = "g/day")
adg
adg$associations[, c("disease", "associated_with", "measure", "value")]
```

### Average daily gain

The first impact table has the loss of average daily gain (in g/day) of
pigs with each disease, compared with pigs without it, and an interaction
row: pigs with both PRRS and MHP lose 15 g/day more than the two diseases
alone would give (`adjusted_for = "all"`). Most rows have a distribution,
so `deconflate()` also draws intervals (200 draws keep this example
fast):

```{r}
res_adg <- deconflate(adg, n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
res_adg
```

Each adjusted impact is smaller than the raw one, because each raw
estimate also carried part of the loss of the diseases that come with it.
The adjusted total, the loss per pig in the population, is the sum of the
contributions; the raw total is what the same estimates give when the
diseases are taken as unrelated.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6}
plot(res_adg, type = "contributions")
```

### Three outcomes, one population

The diseases and associations are the same for every outcome; only the
impact table changes. Emissions are the percentage increase in emission
intensity (kg CO2-equivalent per kg live weight), and welfare the points
lost on a 0-100 welfare index:

```{r}
tables <- list(
  adg = list(file = "impacts_adg.csv", outcome = "average daily gain loss", units = "g/day"),
  environment = list(file = "impacts_environment.csv", outcome = "emission intensity increase",
                     units = "% of kg CO2-eq per kg live weight"),
  welfare = list(file = "impacts_welfare.csv", outcome = "welfare index loss",
                 units = "points on a 0-100 index"))
results <- lapply(tables, function(t) deconflate(read_pigs(t$file, t$outcome, t$units), n_draws = 0))
data.frame(
  outcome = vapply(results, function(r) r$outcome, ""),
  units = vapply(results, function(r) r$units, ""),
  raw = vapply(results, function(r) r$totals$raw_total, 0),
  adjusted = vapply(results, function(r) r$totals$adjusted_total, 0),
  reduction = vapply(results, function(r) 1 - r$totals$adjusted_total / r$totals$raw_total, 0),
  PRRS_share = vapply(results, function(r) r$contributions$share[r$contributions$disease == "PRRS"], 0)
)
```

About a quarter of each raw total is double counting here, and PRRS
accounts for about half of each adjusted total. The outcomes stay in their
own units: converting a loss of daily gain, extra emissions or welfare
points into money, or weighing them against each other, is left to the
user.

### Which inputs matter?

`cm_sensitivity()` varies every input one at a time, including the PCV2-SIV
association that nobody estimated:

```{r}
s <- cm_sensitivity(res_adg)
s
```

Here the PCV2-SIV association moves the total about as much as the MHP
impact does, so an estimate of it would be worth having.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
plot(s)
```

The other tools of the package (thresholds, the diagnosis of the inputs,
summaries and the export table) work the same way as in the dairy
examples; see `vignette("thresholds-and-scaling")` and
`vignette("uncertainty")`.

## People: chronic conditions and hospitalisation

In people, obesity (OBE), hypertension (HTN), type 2 diabetes (T2D) and
chronic kidney disease (CKD) cluster strongly, and each is associated with
a higher risk of hospitalisation. Here the inputs are typed in R rather
than read from files: prevalences in adults of one age band, odds ratios
between the conditions (no estimate for obesity and kidney disease, which
the fit fills in), and the risk of hospitalisation within a year as a
hazard ratio or a risk ratio for each condition. The T2D estimate is
already adjusted for obesity, as is common in such studies.

```{r}
pop <- cm_population(
  cm_diseases(c("OBE", "HTN", "T2D", "CKD"), c(0.30, 0.40, 0.12, 0.10)),
  cm_associations(c("OBE", "OBE", "T2D", "T2D", "HTN"),
                  c("T2D", "HTN", "HTN", "CKD", "CKD"),
                  c(3.0, 2.5, 2.2, 3.0, 2.5)))
hosp <- cm_impacts(c("OBE", "HTN", "T2D", "CKD"), c(1.3, 1.4, 1.8, 2.2),
                   measure = c("RR", "HR", "HR", "HR"),
                   adjusted_for = c(NA, NA, "OBE", NA),
                   outcome = "hospitalisation")
people <- cm_model(pop, hosp)
```

The impacts are event impacts (they have a `measure`), so they are
adjusted with `event_model = TRUE` and the overall risk of the event in the
period, here 10% a year:

```{r}
res_people <- deconflate(people, event_model = TRUE, overall_risk = 0.10)
res_people
```

The adjusted hazard ratios are each condition's own effect. The risk
attributable to the four conditions is split between them. It is smaller
than the raw attributable risk (the conditions taken as unrelated): each raw
estimate also carried part of the effect of the conditions that come with
it, and when conditions cluster, more of their risk falls on the same
people, who can be hospitalised only once.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6}
plot(res_people, type = "contributions")
```

The results are proportions of people hospitalised in the year. Turning
them into numbers of admissions, bed-days or costs is left to the user.

## What changes with the setting

Nothing in the model depends on the species or the outcome. What has to be
checked in each setting is that the inputs fit together:

* All inputs refer to the same period (here a grow-finish period, or a
  year) and the same population. A prevalence in finishing pigs and an
  impact measured in weaners do not belong in one model.
* Each impact table holds one outcome in one unit. Several outcomes are
  several tables, adjusted in turn on the same diseases and associations.
* Impacts on the risk of an event (death, culling, hospitalisation,
  treatment failure) are event impacts; amounts per individual (gain,
  yield, emissions, scores, costs) are additive impacts.
* Estimates adjusted for some of the other diseases say so in
  `adjusted_for`; the model then does not adjust them twice.

`vignette("own-data")` explains the input tables, and
`vignette("event-impacts")` the event model.
